messages.body: two of three now. and the thing is they're not asking for the world, they just want to see what they billed, send an invoice, track whether it got paid. we keep saying the product handles the whole workflow and then they get to the part where money changes hands and we've got nothing. i think this is the seed closer. like genuinely. because right now we're a very nice frontend to their paper invoices

messages.subject: billing
messages.body:
I know they're asking. But billing isn't one feature, it's twelve features pretending to be one. Invoice templates, payment tracking, partial payments, refunds, insurance splits, past-due notices, reporting. Every clinic does it differently and they all think their way is the obvious way.

Six weeks if we're lucky. Probably eight.

messages.subject: billing
messages.body: Then they send the invoice and come back into Thicket and can't see whether it was paid. So now we're the system that knows about the appointment and the records but not the money, which means we're not the system of record anymore, which is the only reason they're tolerating the switch.

messages.subject: billing
messages.body:
If we build it wrong we lose all three, plus the next six months. Billing is the part of the system where being slightly wrong means their bank account is wrong, and when someone's bank account is wrong they don't file a bug report, they leave.

We're at the stage where we should be learning whether the scheduling model works for more than one clinic, whether the records structure makes sense, whether people can actually onboard without us sitting there. Those are product-risk questions. Billing is execution risk on top of a product we haven't proven yet.
